entities.name: Most existing textile drying models focus on convective air drying, creating a gap for modeling the direct-contact, low-pressure heated-cylinder drying process
entities.description: Most existing textile drying models focus on convective air drying, creating a gap for modeling the direct-contact, low-pressure heated-cylinder drying process considered here.
entities.evidence_span: Despite the extensive literature on textile drying, most existing models describe convective drying processes in which air is used as the primary heat and mass transfer medium. The drying process considered in the present work differs significantly from this configuration.

entities.name: The temperature profile through the fabric thickness is governed by a fixed temperature at the cylinder–fabric interface, heat exchange at the opposite surface
entities.description: The temperature profile through the fabric thickness is governed by a fixed temperature at the cylinder–fabric interface, heat exchange at the opposite surface with the environment, conductive heat transfer through the thickness, and energy consumption by evaporation via latent heat.

entities.name: The bell-shaped moisture profile results from the alternating drying-and-flipping sequence: each surface is directly exposed to the heated cylinder during diffe
entities.description: The bell-shaped moisture profile results from the alternating drying-and-flipping sequence: each surface is directly exposed to the heated cylinder during different phases and therefore dries more strongly, while the interior remains less heated and retains more moisture.
entities.evidence_span: This behaviour can be explained by the operating sequence of the drying process. The fabric undergoes three drying phases and is flipped after each phase: it is first dried on side A, then on side B, and finally again on side A. As a consequence, both surfaces are directly exposed to the heated cylinder during the process and experience stronger evaporation, while the inner region remains comparatively less heated.

evidence_spans: This behaviour can be explained by the operating sequence of the drying process. The fabric undergoes three drying phases and is flipped after each phase: it is first dried on side A, then on side B, and finally again on side A. As a consequence, both surfaces are directly exposed to the heated cylinder during the process and experience stronger evaporation, while the inner region remains comparatively less heated.

entities.name: The bell-shaped moisture profile results from the alternating drying-and-flipping sequence: each surface is directly exposed to the heated cylinder during different phases and therefore dries more str
entities.description: The bell-shaped moisture profile results from the alternating drying-and-flipping sequence: each surface is directly exposed to the heated cylinder during different phases and therefore dries more strongly, while the interior remains less heated and retains more moisture.
entities.evidence_span: This behaviour can be explained by the operating sequence of the drying process. The fabric undergoes three drying phases and is flipped after each phase: it is first dried on side A, then on side B, and finally again on side A. As a consequence, both surfaces are directly exposed to the heated cylinder during the process and experience stronger evaporation, while the inner region remains comparatively less heated.

Textile drying is a key operation in the textile production cycle as it represents one of the most energy-
intensive stages and plays a critical role in determining both product quality and overall process
efficiency.

Despite the extensive literature on textile drying, most existing models describe convective drying processes in which air is used as the primary heat and mass transfer medium. The drying process considered in the present work differs significantly from this configuration.
